newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: No end seen on South African currency limits.
newsitem.headline: No end seen on South African currency limits.

text.p: South Africans may have to wait a little longer for an end to restrictions on changing rand into foreign currency because of the country's low reserves of foreign money, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Friday.
Stals, speaking at an economic conference, said it could be a catastrophe to allow a rush of people to change rand when government stocks of other currencies were so low.
Lifting limits on currency exchange is critical if the government is to give South African residents premission to invest savings outside the country.
South Africans, who have long waited for the restrictions to be lifted, currently only can get foreign currency -- and then limited amounts -- when they travel abroad.

"When South African residents are given permission to invest their rand savings outside the country, there must be some reasonable assurance that it will be possible for them to convert rand assets into foreign currencies with which they can acquire foreign investment," Stals said.
South African reserves declined from 15.7 billion rand ($3.4 billion) at the end of 1995 to 10.0 billion rand at the end of September, equivalent to four weeks import cover.

President Nelson Mandela's government has committed itself to scrapping the exchange-rate controls, a step seen by financial markets as vital for South Africa's complete integration into the global economy.

The rand, trading at 3.65 to the dollar at the start of the year, has slumped by almost 20 percent and on Friday was at 4.585 bid to the dollar, hovering just above its lowest level of 4.59 hit in August.

Stals said the exchange-control problem was "very well understood" by the central bank, which was forced to close the foreign exchange market in August 1985 and introduce a moratorium on the repayment of international commitments.
He criticised commentators who suggested South Africa would abolish all remaining controls in a "big bang" approach, saying this was creating false expectations and unnecessary fears.
